newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile, European scientists sign telescope deal.
newsitem.headline: Chile, European scientists sign telescope deal.

text.p: Chile and the European Southern Observatory signed on Monday an agreement to clarify loopholes in an earlier treaty that sparked a dispute over a huge telescope the agency is building in the Atacama Desert.
"We know that this document is the end of a process which was not always easy and which resulted in various difficulties in our country," Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza said.
"(But) we have both given a sign of willingness to cooperate to resolve disputes and from this point of view I am sure that what we do in the future will be on the same lines."

The agreement, which modifies a treaty signed in 1963, clarifies the ESO's legal status and guarantees Chilean astronomers access to up to 10 percent of observation time at all of the agency's telescopes in Chile.

A legal dispute over land rights led to a court order halting building work at the $500 million telescope, known as Cerro Paranal, which will be the largest in the world when it is finished early next century.

The European scientists ignored the ruling, inciting local officials and police to enter the grounds forcibly to inspect the site. Agency officials protested and accused the government of violating its legal rights.

The court case was settled recently with the government paying compensation to a local family who claimed the telescope was being built on their land. Built on a parched mountain top, the observatory is being funded by the governments of Germany, France, Italy, Denmark, Switzerland, Belgium, Sweden and the Netherlands.
Sweden's King Carl Gustav and Queen Silvia will visit the half-built telescope this week as part of an official visit to Chile.

Three other giant astronomical complexes, one of them run by the ESO and the others by U.S. groups, operate in Chile's barren north where scientists are attracted by the crisp air and cloudless skies.
